raw_case_text:
A 13-year-old girl diagnosed the previous year with CVID in the setting of pneumonia, low serum immunoglobulin levels, and absent antibody responses to immunizations, presented with worsening dyspnea. Whole exome sequencing did not reveal an underlying genetic explanation for the immune deficiency. A chest CT scan at the time of CVID diagnosis revealed only mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She was placed on monthly IgG replacement therapy and did well until she reported gradual worsening of dyspnea over 3 months. The dyspnea first manifested during competitive sports and progressed to an inability to walk up a single flight of stairs. Pulmonary function testing results (Table 1) showed a restrictive pattern, and she was unable to complete the maneuvers for diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). A follow-up chest CT scan revealed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, peripheral interlobular septal thickening, peripheral consolidation, and ground glass opacities (Figure 1). Bronchoalveolar lavage obtained by bronchoscopy did not show any evidence of infection. Specific testing included bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral cultures along with PCR assays for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpes virus-8, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. She underwent a right lower lobe wedge resection biopsy via thoracoscopy. The biopsy (Figure 2) showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with aggregates of small lymphocytes, scattered multinucleated giant cells, scattered foci of organizing pneumonia, interstitial fibrosis focally in the subpleural space but not prominent or diffuse, and airway luminal compromise from adjacent lymphoid hyperplasia, confirming the diagnosis of GLILD.
She was treated with 4 doses of rituximab 375 mg/m2 given 4-6 months apart, based on clinical symptoms and pulmonary function testing, and azathioprine 50 mg daily for 18 months as IgG replacement therapy was continued. She responded well to the new therapy regimen with complete resolution of exercise intolerance and normalization of pulmonary function testing parameters (Table 1). She also had remarkable improvement of the CT scan abnormalities (Figure 1) with the follow up CT scan after completion of therapy demonstrating resolution of all abnormalities.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-year-old girl with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) on monthly immunoglobulin replacement therapy presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 1 year earlier with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID; low serum immunoglobulins, absent vaccine antibody responses, negative whole-exome sequencing, and isolated mediastinal lymphadenopathy on baseline chest CT), the patient had initially done well on monthly intravenous/subcutaneous IgG replacement therapy. Over the 3 months preceding presentation, she developed progressive exertional dyspnea that first appeared during competitive sports and worsened until she was unable to climb a single flight of stairs.
subjective.past_medical_history: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) diagnosed at age 12 following pneumonia; negative whole-exome sequencing for monogenic immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive exertional dyspnea and severe exercise intolerance over 3 months. Home medication was monthly IgG replacement therapy.

objective.physical_examination: Severe exercise intolerance (unable to walk up one flight of stairs).
objective.routine_investigations: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Restrictive ventilatory defect (unable to complete DLCO maneuvers at baseline; PFTs completely normalized following combination therapy).
objective.advanced_workup: Follow-up chest CT scan: Mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, peripheral interlobular septal thickening, peripheral consolidations, and ground-glass opacities. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Negative bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral cultures, and negative PCR assays for Pneumocystis jirovecii, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, CMV, EBV, and HHV-8. Thoracoscopic right lower lobe wedge biopsy: Non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with aggregates of small lymphocytes, scattered multinucleated giant cells, focal organizing pneumonia, focal subpleural interstitial fibrosis, and peribronchiolar lymphoid hyperplasia compromising airway lumina, confirming granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD) complicating common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), definitively confirmed by thoracoscopic right lower lobe wedge biopsy after excluding Pneumocystis jirovecii, viral, fungal, and mycobacterial infections on BAL. Plan and clinical course: Treated with four doses of intravenous rituximab (375 mg/m2 administered every 4–6 months) combined with daily oral azathioprine (50 mg/day for 18 months) while continuing monthly IgG replacement therapy, resulting in complete resolution of exercise intolerance, normalization of pulmonary function tests, and complete clearance of CT abnormalities.
